Microbial Association Network with NetCoMi

11-Jun-2025


Organisation: Data Science Platform
Responsibles: Alberto Pallejà Caro (apca@biosustain.dtu.dk)
Sebastian Ayala Ruano (asaru@dtu.dk)
Juliana Assis (jasge@dtu.dk)


This markdown is to create microbial association networks (MANs) based on the abundance data using the the NetCoMi package.

1 Work environment setup

1.1 Import R Packages

library(NetCoMi)
library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)

1.2 Load data

# Abundance table
abundance <- readRDS(file = "../data/MetaphlanAbundance_Species.rds")
rownames(abundance) <- gsub("_SRR_db1.metaphlan", "", rownames(abundance))
dim(abundance)
## [1]  18 293
# Taxonomical annotation
annotation <- readRDS(file = "../data/MetaphlanAnnotations_Species.rds")
dim(annotation)
## [1] 293   7
# Metadata
metadata <- read.table(file = "../data/metadata.tsv",
                       header = TRUE, sep = "\t",
                       quote = "",
                       row.names = NULL)
rownames(metadata) <- metadata$Sample
dim(metadata)
## [1] 18 21
# Take only samples with sequencing and metadata information
abundance <- abundance[rownames(abundance) %in% rownames(metadata),]
dim(abundance)
## [1]  18 293
# Replace the column names of the abundance table with the species names
colnames(abundance) <- annotation$species[match(colnames(abundance), rownames(annotation))]

1.3 Create a directory to store the results

results_dir <- "results/report/05_Microbial-association-networks"

dir.create(results_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

2 Network construction

We create a Microbial association network (MAN) with the Correlation inference for Compositional data through Lasso (CCLasso) method. CCLasso estimates positive definite Pearson correlations from log-ratio variances using a latent variable model based on least squares with an L1 penalty. Aitchison introduced log-ratios as a basis for analyzing compositional data, as these values are independent of the total sum of counts. Consequently, CCLasso addresses the compositional nature of metagenomics data.

The netConstruct() function is used to build the network. To make the calculations feasible, we filter the taxa to the 50 most abundant species using the filtTax and filtTaxPar parameters.

Normalization is performed internally as part of the CCLasso method, so we set normMethod to none. To handle zeros in the data, we applied the pseudoZO method, which adds a pseudo count of 1 to zero values.

The signed method was aplied for transforming associationss into dissimilarities, so that strongly negatively associated taxa have a high dissimilarity and, in turn, a low similarity, which corresponds to edge weights in the network plot.

A threshold of 0.5 is applied as sparsification method, meaning that only species with a correlation greater than or equal to 0.5 will be included in the network.

The verbose argument is set to 3 so that all messages generated by netConstruct() as well as messages of external functions are printed. Finally, we set a seed for reproducibility.

net_cclasso <- netConstruct(abundance,
                           measure = "cclasso",
                           filtTax = "highestFreq",
                           filtTaxPar = list(highestFreq = 50),
                           normMethod = "none",
                           zeroMethod = "pseudoZO",
                           dissFunc = "signed",
                           sparsMethod = "threshold",
                           thresh = 0.5,
                           verbose = 3,
                           seed = 2236)

Now, we can check and save the edge list of the network. It contains the estimated associations, dissmiliarities, and similarities (adj column) for each pair of species.

head(net_cclasso$edgelist1)
write.table(net_cclasso$edgelist1, 
            file = file.path(results_dir, "1_cclasso_network_edgelist.csv"),
            sep = ",", quote = FALSE, row.names = FALSE)

We can also use theplotHeat function to plot the estimated associations.

# Generate the plot
heatmap <- plotHeat(net_cclasso$assoMat1, textUpp = "none", textLow = "none")

# Open and close PNG device
png(file.path(results_dir, "2_cclasso_network_association_heatmap.png"), width = 2000, height = 1800, res = 150)
dev.off()
## quartz_off_screen 
##                 2

3 Network analysis

The netAnalyze() function is used for analyzing the MAN.

Here, centrLCC is set to FALSE, so the centralities are calculated for all nodes in the network, not only for those in the largest connected component (LCC). weightDeg and normDeg are set to FALSE, so that the degree of a node is simply defined as the number of connections it has to other nodes.

Hubs are defined here as nodes with a degree above the 90% quantile of the empirical degree distribution, which is specified by the hubPar and hubQuant arguments.

Clusters are identified using the greedy modularity optimization algorithm (cluster_fast_greedy). This algorithm optimize the modularity of networks by iteratively grouping nodes into communities, aiming to maximize the density of intra-community edges compared to inter-community edges

props_cclasso <- netAnalyze(net_cclasso, 
                            # Centrality
                            centrLCC = FALSE,
                            weightDeg = FALSE,
                            normDeg = FALSE,
                            
                            # Hubs
                            hubPar = "degree",
                            hubQuant = 0.9,
                            
                            # Clustering
                            clustMethod = "cluster_fast_greedy"
                    )

# Print the summary of the network analysis
summary(props_cclasso, numbNodes = 5L)

4 Network visualization

Finally, we can visualize the network using the plot() function.

# Generate the plot
net_viz <- plot(props_cclasso,
     # Network
     layout = "spring",
     repulsion = 0.9,
     title1 = "CCLasso Network",
     showTitle = TRUE,
     rmSingles = TRUE,
     cexTitle = 1,

     # Nodes 
     nodeColor = "cluster", 
     nodeSize = "degree",
     cexNodes = 2.7, 
     nodeSizeSpread = 2,
     shortenLabels = "simple",
     labelLength = 8L,

     # Edges
     posCol = "#ac1214", # red
     negCol ="#0d1fad", # blue
)

legend(0.7, 1.1, title = "Estimated associations:", legend = c("+","-"), 
        col = c("#ac1214","#0d1fad"), inset = 0.02, cex = 0.8, lty = 1, lwd = 3.5, 
        bty = "n", horiz = TRUE, y.intersp = 0.7)

# Open and close PNG device
png(file.path(results_dir, "3_cclasso_network.png"), width = 2500, height = 2300, res = 150)
dev.off()

5 Further information

The Network learning & analysis chapter from the Orchestrating Microbiome Analysis Book provides more details about all the steps and consideration to take when creating and analyzing microbial association networks (MANs).
